entries.title: Two black holes spiral inward
entries.body:
Numerical replay.

Watch the two black holes orbit their shared centre. Gravitational waves carry energy and angular momentum away, bringing the pair closer. This representative numerical binary is inspired by GW150914. Move around the paused scene to compare their positions and sizes; changing your viewpoint leaves the selected event time unchanged.

entries.title: Inspiral and tidal gas
entries.body:
Assumed gas environment.

Look for uneven bright patches and stretched gas around each black hole. Pressure and tidal gravity reshape the recorded fluid. The patches follow passive material labels carried by that flow, rather than independent glowing particles. View the disks from above and below to see how curved light reveals the far side.

entries.title: The final approach accelerates
entries.body:
One shared source clock.

The black holes are closer and their orbital motion is faster. The gravitational wave frequency rises: this is the chirp. Raise the wrist display to compare the signal with the pair. Automatic slow motion makes this interval easier to inspect, while bodies, gas and waveform still share the same event time.

entries.bodyExperiment:
Illustrative late evolution.

The pair is approaching the joining transition. In this adjustable experiment, the quantitative inspiral ends at ten gravitational radii. Later positions and the merger provide an illustrative continuation. The wrist leaves unsupported signal values unavailable. Explore the gas and dark regions, and compare an earlier supported time to see the rising inspiral frequency.

entries.title: A common black hole forms
entries.body:
Illustrative capture surface.

The two dark regions are joining. At this stage the numerical record identifies a common horizon, and one remnant replaces the pair. The smooth visible boundary helps you follow that transition. Inspect it from another angle; the recorded body and waveform values continue to use the same scientific history.

Illustrative merger.

Inspect the smooth boundary from another angle. Gas continues through its own reduced calculation while the wrist makes unavailable signal predictions explicit.

entries.title: The remnant settles
entries.body:
Finite assumed gas inventory.

One black hole remains as the gravitational wave signal fades through ringdown. Look for the changing gas and its declining brightness. This scene begins with a finite amount of gas and does not continually refill it. Pause or rewind to compare earlier structure, and explore the remnant freely from different viewpoints.

entries.title: The GW150914 system
entries.body:
Representative reconstruction.

GW150914 was the first gravitational wave signal detected directly, recorded by LIGO in 2015. It revealed two black holes merging into one. This exhibit uses a representative numerical binary to explore that event. The bright gas is an assumed environment added for exploration, rather than a disk measured around GW150914.
entries.narration: This system is inspired by G W fifteen oh nine fourteen, the first gravitational wave signal detected directly by LIGO in twenty fifteen. It revealed two black holes merging into one. The exhibit uses a representative numerical binary. Its bright gas is an assumed environment, rather than an observed disk.

entries.title: Black hole A
entries.body:
Approximate capture region.

This is black hole A. Its mass sets its gravitational length scale and the size of the displayed dark region. A black hole is not a solid sphere. Compare its mass with component B on the wrist. Move sideways to inspect the silhouette against the assumed gas shining behind and around it.

entries.title: Black hole B
entries.body:
The second component.

This is black hole B. Compare its mass and displayed dark region with component A, then follow how both orbit their shared centre. The two bodies form one interacting system. Their changing motion produces gravitational waves. The bright assumed gas helps make their surroundings visible, but the binary remains the source of the waveform.

entries.title: The accretion disks
entries.body:
Assumed gas and colour.

The bright structures represent rotating gas around the black holes. Their coarse density and motion evolve through pressure, softened gravity and accretion sinks. Flowing patches add visible material detail without changing that gas calculation. Look above, below and along the disk plane: emission, absorption and approximate light bending change what you see.
entries.narration: These bright structures represent assumed gas rotating around the black holes. Pressure and softened gravity evolve its flow, while sinks remove nearby gas. Bright patches add material detail. Look above, below, and along the disk plane to see how emission, absorption, and approximate light bending change your view.

entries.title: The rippling light display
entries.body:
Exaggerated wave display.

Gravitational waves are travelling changes in spacetime. The moving ripples in the background visualize the retained waveform history through an optical illustration. Their displacement is amplified and their spacing compressed to make them visible. Compare the wrist signal and wave map; this is not a literal view of visible waves around GW150914.
